content_text: [1/2 @gregoryblotnick] "swinging swords like Shinobi" / destroying your best loved ideas 1/4 this was a real good tweet, or at least one that has been lodged in my mind....because more and more, in DMs/texts or on the phone, I find myself responding with a mix of what I personally know + a mix of follow up LLM prompts. basically the goal is to give the best possible answer and that's going to be a mix of the two above - but the shift in the proportions (or what the right proportions are) is what I'm getting at 2/4 because what I seem to find...is that "what I know" gets smaller and smaller relative to what LLM's know. the catch is that this is never obvious up front, it never pops out in the first prompt or query it always takes some coaxing or wheedling, 2-3 follow-on prompts, just swinging swords and chopping away at that bitch but as LLMs get better and better...that answer is gonna pop out. I see this firsthand over the last 6-12 months, esp with anything finance/markets related, where stuff I used to say "I'm not sure on these LLMs" about...those answers are now coming back 100% perfect. 3/4 for a rational human being, the thought of this should be somewhat terrifying i.e. "I don't actually know anything the LLMs don't know" or "I have no unique domain expertise" or "the robots have eaten my brain" but in the quest to give the best possible answer, like, I've found it worth the time to just sit there and compile some list of "wtf do I think I know" and then just bash away to see if what you know, is actually out there in LLM land, absorbed into the jungian collective unconscious because its to the benefit of the answer recipient...the unquestionable advantage of LLMs are that the other person can ask as many follow up q's as they like, even ones where they're worried about looking stupid. 4/4 so you can stroke your ego by giving them a 10 minute B+ answer, "look how smart I am," or by doing this kind of work you can hit them with a paragraph or two and then 2-3 prompts, usually ones you've tested yourself -- i.e. "these led me to a thorough and well-written answer very quickly" the truth, I think, is that you dont really know less than you do...a lot of what you know, should be based on a series of logical premises. so in the series of prompts or queries to an LLM to get at "what you know" -- munger's "destroying your best loved ideas" -- what you are really doing is just leading it down the same worldview-assembly-line, step by step, the same way you would another human. and LLMs are just as good (if not way better) at following this trail of inquiry END there is a quote from one of Bacon's essays, I think the one on counsel, on how "dry light is the best" -- paraphrasing heraclitus he's talking about how in theory, a friend or someone you keep as close counsel is going to shit you straight, or as straight as possible, relative to the rest of the world but even then...all humans suffer from "wet light" you could say, meaning, our thought patterns and subconscious are drenched in preconceived notions, biases, ways we view the world which are invisible to us and so to the intrepid introvert, or someone who is really trying to figure out "what the fuck do I really know," LLMs are such a blessing because the more harsh you ask for the feedback, the more critical you want them to be, the more u say like the philosopher king ODB did..."ooo baby I like it raw"...trust that they are going to give it to you ad infinitum lol unlimited heat. the driest light available in the history of humanity, and only getting drier. (link to Francis Bacon's "essays" - https://www.gutenberg.org/files/56463/56463-h/56463-h.htm) --- [2/2 @gregoryblotnick] this post here is the relevant one...really good feedback from ppl so far, probably in need of a Part Two soon. https://x.com/gregoryblotnick/status/2067593785194733972?s=20
